articles.title: Why Your Playwright Tests Keep Breaking (And How Vision LLMs Are Fixing Web Automation Forever)
articles.excerpt: If you have spent any significant amount of time maintaining end-to-end (E2E) test suites or web scraping pipelines, you are intimately familiar with the fragility of modern web automation. For over a…
articles.body: If you have spent any significant amount of time maintaining end-to-end (E2E) test suites or web scraping pipelines, you are intimately familiar with the fragility of modern web automation. For over a decade, our industry has relied on static, hardcoded locators: XPath expressions, complex CSS selectors, and DOM attribute queries like data-testid="submit-button" . This architecture was built on a comforting, deterministic assumption: that a developer's intent has a rigid, unyielding relationship with the Document Object Model (DOM). That assumption is entirely dead. Modern single-page applications (SPAs), heavily abstracted component libraries, shadow DOMs, randomized class names generated by CSS modules, and complex canvas-based renderings have rendered traditional locators obsolete.

articles.title: I Taught 200+ Beginners to Code. Here Is What It Taught Me About Writing Better Software
articles.excerpt: I have taught hundreds of beginner developers through CTROTECH over the past few years. I expected to help them learn. I did not expect they would make me a better engineer. Here is the pattern I noti…
articles.body: I have taught hundreds of beginner developers through CTROTECH over the past few years. I expected to help them learn. I did not expect they would make me a better engineer. Here is the pattern I noticed: every time a student struggled with something, it revealed an assumption I had been making in my own code. Fixing those assumptions made my code better. This article is about five specific patterns I observed across hundreds of students and how they changed the way I write software. Pattern 1: Beginners Struggle with Implicit Behavior When students first learn JavaScript, implicit returns cause a lot of confusion. const double = ( x ) => x * 2 The confusion comes from implicit behavior, not from the arrow function syntax itself. The function returns without a return keyword.

articles.body: Which model actually writes better TypeScript, and does it matter enough to change what you reach for? I ran Claude Fable 5 and GPT-4o through the same set of TypeScript generation tasks to find out, and the answer is more useful than a leaderboard number: each model has a different failure mode, and which one bites you depends on what you are building. I do a fair amount of AI systems architecture work, and picking the right model for codegen inside a pipeline is a decision that compounds. Get it wrong and you are paying for review time on every generated PR. Here is what actually held up under test. How I set up the test (apples to apples methodology) I kept the test as fair as I could make it. Both models got the same prompts, the same grading rubric, and no retries.

articles.body: Things aren't going so well for NASA's latest satellite rescue mission. NASA launched the Swift Boost mission on July 3, sending a specialized spacecraft to low Earth orbit on the final flight of Northrop Grumman's air-launched Pegasus XL rocket. The spacecraft is called LINK and was built by Arizona-based Katalyst Space Technologies. LINK was sent to orbit to try and link up with NASA's Swift observatory , a highly successful scientific satellite designed to search for gamma-ray bursts , some of the most energetic events in the universe. But it looks like just a few weeks after launch, LINK is experiencing some issues.

articles.excerpt: A genuinely pocket-sized smart telescope
articles.body: The best smart telescopes have transformed astrophotography over the past few years, combining small telescope optics and automated mounts with dashcam-style camera sensors and image-processing software. The result? Compact devices that can be controlled entirely from a smartphone. Impressively, the DwarfLab Dwarf Mini pushes that concept even further. Roughly the size of a thick paperback book, it’s one of the smallest smart telescopes yet produced — tiny enough to fit in a jacket pocket while still capable of imaging nebulae, star clusters, the moon and even sunspots. It's also one of the best telescopes for beginners . Positioned below the larger Dwarf 3 in DwarfLab’s lineup, the Mini sacrifices aperture and resolution for portability.

articles.title: 'The Ark' creator Dean Devlin talks season 3's enormous mystery box and sci-fi surprises (interview)
articles.excerpt: "We went wildly over budget and just made the biggest craziest season we could possible imagine."
articles.body: SYFY’s optimistic space opera series, " The Ark ," embarks upon its third thrilling season today, occupying a unique entertainment spot as the only weekly scripted sci-fi series currently on regular broadcast television. With an impressive creative resume featuring executive producers Dean Devlin ("Stargate," "Independence Day") and Jonathan Glassner ("Stargate SG-1") and a hopeful premise about humanity’s search for a new home amid the stars, it’s a refreshing show perfect for a laidback, summertime watch. Season 3 delivers more dangerous exoplanets inhabited by ravenous toothy monsters, the mystery of an alien stone tablet, and Captain Sharon Garnet’s Ark One searching for long-lost colonists. We caught up with Devlin to find out more about this third outing.
